question.value: Generate a multiwavelength catalog and classification framework of 10 and 21 um compact mid-infrared sources in 19 nearby PHANGS-JWST galaxies to study young stellar clusters and evolved dusty stars.

evidence.quote: In this paper, we present catalogs of compact sources emitting at 10 and 21 $\mu$m in JWST imaging of 19 nearby galaxies ($D = 5$-20 Mpc).
In this work, we develop a photometric method and establish a classification framework for these compact sources.
ADS/JAO.ALMA#2018.A.00062.S,

We used CO (2-1) emission line maps from the PHANGS–ALMA project (cite: Leroy2021).

provided.value: Imaging in eight filters (F200W, F300M, F335M, F360M, F770W, F1000W, F1130W, F2100W) under program 2107

evidence.quote: The PHANGS–JWST observations were obtained under JWST program 2107 (PI: J. Lee) .
The imaging program used NIRCam and MIRI in eight filters spanning central wavelengths from 2, 3, 3.3, 3.6, 7.7, 10, 11.3, to 21 $\mu$m (cite: lee2023).

provided.value: Broadband imaging in F275W, F336W, F438W, F555W, F814W and narrowband Halpha in F657N or F658N

evidence.quote: These observations were conducted using the WFC3/UVIS camera in parallel mode with ACS/WFC (Cycle 26, PID 15654), utilizing the filter set F275W (NUV), F336W (U), F438W (B), F555W (V), and F814W (I).
The survey imaged galaxies with the WFC3 camera using either the F657N or F658N filter, depending on redshift.

provided.value: Optical IFU spectroscopy (4800 to 9300 A), emission line maps (Halpha, Hbeta, etc.), E(B-V) reddening maps, and Halpha equivalent width

evidence.quote: We also incorporated data from the PHANGS-MUSE survey (program IDs: 1100.B-0651, PI: E. Schinnerer; 095.C-0473, PI: G. Blanc; and 094.C-0623, PI: K. Kreckel).
In particular, we rely on H$\alpha$ and H$\beta$ emission line maps that are corrected for the Milky Way Foreground extinction as well as the $E(B-V)$ reddening maps from (cite: Belfiore2023)
We also use the stellar continuum of the MUSE data combined with the H$\alpha$ to measure the H$\alpha$ equivalent width (EW)

provided.value: 3.6 um images used to derive morphological masks of sub-galactic environments

evidence.quote: We further use the morphological masks of sub-galactic environments from (cite: Querejeta2021).
These maps are derived from Spitzer 3.6 $\mu$m images and classify different environments within our sample, including the center, bar, spiral arms, interarm regions, and the disk.

provided.value: Astrometry (DR2) and foreground star identification via parallax (DR3)

evidence.quote: All images were drizzled and aligned to the native pixel scale of WFC3, which is 0.04$''$ and the astrometry was established using GAIA DR2 sources (cite: GaiaMission).
We cross-matched both catalogs with the *Gaia* Data Release (DR3) survey to detect potential contamination from foreground stars (FGs) (cite: GaiaMission).

what.value: CO(2-1) emission line maps and galaxy properties

evidence.quote: We used CO (2-1) emission line maps from the PHANGS–ALMA project (cite: Leroy2021).
Table [\[tab:galaxies\]](#tab:galaxies) lists the galaxies included in this study along with their properties, as reported in (cite: lee2023) and (cite: Leroy2021).
We further use the morphological masks of sub-galactic environments from (cite: Querejeta2021).

what.value: MUSE emission line maps and stellar continuum

evidence.quote: For this work, we use emission line maps from (cite: phangs-muse), which were generated using the MUSE Data Analysis Pipeline (DAP).
In particular, we rely on H$\alpha$ and H$\beta$ emission line maps that are corrected for the Milky Way Foreground extinction as well as the $E(B-V)$ reddening maps from (cite: Belfiore2023)

what.value: SAGE-LMC spectroscopic classifications and photometric catalogs of evolved stars

evidence.quote: We use the `PARSEC` stellar evolutionary tracks (section [4.1.2](#sec:parsec)) to classify RSGs, O-AGBs, and C-AGBs, which we validate with observations from the SAGE-LMC survey (cite: Jones2017; Jones2018).

By cross-matching our exposed sources with the “nebular” catalog from (cite: neb_catalog) using a maximum separation of 1$''$ (comparable to the typical MUSE PSF), we find that about 77% of the exposed clusters are associated with MUSE nebular regions across our sample of 19 galaxies.

simulations_or_models_as_data.value: CIGALE models of young stellar clusters (using BC03 simple stellar population, Chabrier IMF, Draine & Li dust emission)

evidence.quote: We use the `CIGALE` code to generate models for young stellar clusters (cite: cigale).

simulations_or_models_as_data.value: PARSEC v1.2s and COLIBRI stellar evolutionary tracks for RSGs, O-AGBs, and C-AGBs

evidence.quote: We base our analysis on `PARSEC` v1.2s tracks, which model the evolution of stars with metallicities ranging from $0.0001 \leq Z \leq 0.02$ for masses $0.1 \leq M/M_\odot < 350$, $0.03 \leq Z \leq 0.04$ for $0.1 \leq M/M_\odot < 150$, and $Z = 0.06$ for $0.1 \leq M/M_\odot < 20$ (cite: chen2014; chen2015; Tang).
For stars in the thermally pulsating AGB (TP-AGB) phase, we incorporate the TP-AGB evolution using the COLIBRI code (cite: Pastorelli2019; Pastorelli2020; Marigo; Rosenfield).

archive_products_used_as_is.value: used pre-processed PHANGS-ALMA CO(2-1) emission line maps

evidence.quote: We used CO (2-1) emission line maps from the PHANGS–ALMA project (cite: Leroy2021).
This paper makes use of the following ALMA data, which have been processed as part of the PHANGS–ALMA CO (2-1) survey:
The ALMA beam size varies from 0.74$''$ to 1.81$''$ across different targets.

final_rms.value: ~6.2 mJy beam^-1 (~0.17 K) in 2.5 km s^-1 channels

evidence.quote: The typical 1$\sigma$ noise level in the spectral cubes for all targets is $\sim 6.2$ mJy beam$^{-1}$ at the native resolution, corresponding to a brightness temperature of $\sim 0.17$ K.

what.value: ALMA CO(2-1) data processing and maps

evidence.quote: We used CO (2-1) emission line maps from the PHANGS–ALMA project (cite: Leroy2021).

We use the data reduction pipeline `pjpipe`, described in (cite: Williams2024), which reduces $1/f$ noise in NIRCam, improves background flux consistency, and provides better calibration for both relative and absolute astrometry compared to MAST images

what.value: Dendrogram-based source identification approach and handling of diffraction structures

evidence.quote: Given the limitations of the source-finding algorithms discussed above, we adopt a dendrogram-based approach for source identification, following (cite: Williams) and (cite: hassani23).
More details about the handling of these sources are provided in (cite: hassani23).
We follow the prescription provided by (cite: Johnson_23), using the `PARSEC` tracks to follow the evolution of stars from ages of 1 to 40 Myr with a timestep of 0.1 Myr.

unstated_but_needed: Exact PHANGS-ALMA CO(2-1) data release version and moment-0 map masking scheme (e.g., strict vs. broad mask) sampled for the catalog CO surface brightness

analysis_steps.goal: Convolve multiwavelength JWST and HST images to common catalog resolutions and subtract diffuse emission

method.value: Convolve maps to 0.36'' (F1130W) for the 10 um catalog and 0.67'' (F2100W) for the 21 um catalog using jwst_kernels, mask saturated galaxy centers in NGC 1365 and NGC 7496 using STPSF, and decompose F1000W and F2100W maps using Constrained Diffusion (CD)

evidence.quote: For a 10 $\mu$m catalog, all maps are convolved to match the resolution of the F1130W filter (0.36$''$) using the `jwst_kernels` code.
Similarly, for the 21 $\mu$m catalog, we convolve all maps to the resolution of F2100W (0.67$''$).
In this study, we use Constrained Diffusion (cite: Li2022), a related approach that ensures the sum of all decomposed component fluxes matches the original input map and are non-negative.

key_parameters.value: Use scale 2 of CD decomposition for F2100W and sum of scales 1 and 2 for F1000W; central mask radius ~18'' for NGC 1365 and NGC 7496

evidence.quote: In this study, we use the second scale of our F2100W images for source detection in the 21 $\mu$m maps, as smaller scales are dominated by pixel-to-pixel noise.
In the case of the 10 $\mu$m maps, we used the sum of the first and second scales, which improved the detection of faint sources.
The radius of the masked region is approximately 18$''$.

validation.value: Compared CD-filtered native resolution maps against maps convolved to 0.85'' and previous unfiltered catalog from (cite: hassani23)

evidence.quote: We compare the second component of our F2100W maps with the sum of the 0, 1, and 2 components from the F2100W maps convolved to 0.85$\ensuremath{''}$ in (cite: Pathak2024).

analysis_steps.goal: Identify compact 10 and 21 um sources and measure multiwavelength photometry and completeness limits

method.value: Run ASTRODENDRO on CD-filtered F1000W and F2100W maps, measure peak surface brightness on unfiltered convolved JWST/HST maps with annular background subtraction, sample native ALMA CO(2-1) and MUSE maps at source positions, and run artificial source tests (AST)

evidence.quote: We use the ASTRODENDRO package to identify and measure the structure of mid-infrared emission peaks.

After subtracting the median background, we convert the background-subtracted surface brightness to flux units ($\mu$Jy) by multiplying it by the solid angle subtended by the target PSF (see Table 4 of (cite: lee2023)), which was calculated using the STPSF package (cite: Perrin).
We also included the surface brightness of CO(2-1) and H$\alpha$ EW from (cite: Leroy2021) and MUSE data from (cite: phangs-muse), respectively.

key_parameters.value: Dendrogram threshold = min + 5 * step; min_npix = 41 (F2100W) or 10 (F1000W); min_delta = 3 * step; min separation = 0.33'' (F1000W) or 0.17'' (F2100W); background annulus = 2x to 3x PSF size

evidence.quote: By scaling this step by a factor of 5, the function ensures that only features significantly brighter than the background noise are included in the analysis.

We adopt three criteria to define independent structures: (1) each leaf must contain at least as many pixels as the area subtended by the PSF, which corresponds to $\sim$ 41 pixels for F2100W and $\sim$ 10 pixels for F1000W, calculated from the PSF FWHM (cite: lee2023), (2) the difference between the minimum value in a leaf and the peak intensity is at least three times as large as the “step” size defined previously, and (3) the local maximum of the leaf is separated by all other local maxima by at least one half-width of the PSF for the band we are using: 0.33$''$ ($\sim$3 pixels) for F1000W and 0.17$''$ ($\sim$1.5 pixels) for F2100W.
The background was estimated using an annulus with radii set to $2\times$ and $3\times$ the PSF size: 1.34$''$ and 2.01$''$ for the F2100W catalog, and 0.72$''$ and 1.08$''$ for the F1000W catalog.

fitting.value: Fit detection probability P(f_nu) of 2000 injected fake sources per galaxy with a logistic function to determine 50% completeness limit c2

evidence.quote: We assess the recovery rate of injected fake sources in relation to their flux by fitting the probability of detection $P$ with a logistic function

validation.value: Evaluated completeness limits across sub-galactic environments and local background bins

evidence.quote: We specifically check whether the completeness limit varies with local background level by dividing the data into four bins of background level (units of MJy/sr): $(0, 10^{-0.5})$, $(10^{-0.5}, 1)$, $(1, 10^{0.5})$, and $(10^{0.5}, \infty)$, then calculating the completeness limit for fake sources within these background ranges.

analysis_steps.goal: Classify sources and analyze correlations and luminosity functions

method.value: Classify sources into exposed/embedded young clusters, RSGs, O-AGBs, C-AGBs, CPNs, B[e], WRs, foreground stars, and background galaxies using flux ratio cuts from CIGALE, PARSEC/COLIBRI, and SAGE-LMC; fit Halpha-F2100W linear relation and Pareto-lognormal luminosity functions

evidence.quote: We use the `CIGALE` code (section [4.1.1](#sec:s_cigale)) to model dusty, young stellar clusters and establish band ratio thresholds to find “ISM sources” that we divide into optically exposed or embedded based on the presence of H$\alpha$ emission (Section [4.2](#sec:ismsources)).

We use the `PARSEC` stellar evolutionary tracks (section [4.1.2](#sec:parsec)) to classify RSGs, O-AGBs, and C-AGBs, which we validate with observations from the SAGE-LMC survey (cite: Jones2017; Jones2018).
To characterize the slope of the luminosity functions, we employ a Pareto-lognormal model to fit over distribution.

key_parameters.value: Flux ratio cuts in Table 3; Gaia DR3 parallax_over_error > 3 within 2''; F200W semi-major/semi-minor axis ratio > 1.5 for background galaxies

evidence.quote: Table [\[tab:flux_ratios_sources\]](#tab:flux_ratios_sources) presents the source classifications used in the catalog.

We applied the criterion $\texttt{parallax\_over\_error} > 3$ to identify foreground stars and performed a cross-match with our 10 and 21 $\mu$m catalogs using a 2$\ensuremath{''}$ separation to account for proper motion.
We select elongated F200W sources with a semi-major to semi-minor axis ratio greater than 1.5.

assumptions.value: BC03 SSP with Z=0.02, Chabrier IMF, A_V = 1 and 10 mag, R_V = 3.1, q_PAH = 0.95 to 3.8%, U_min = 10, alpha = 2 for CIGALE cluster models; Kroupa IMF for PARSEC models

evidence.quote: We adopt the BC03 stellar population synthesis models from (cite: Bruzual03) with a metallicity of $Z = 0.02$ and a Chabrier initial mass function (cite: Chabrier).

We also incorporate the dust emission model from (cite: DraineLi2007; Draine2014), considering a PAH mass fraction, $q_{\mathrm{PAH}}$, ranging from 0.95 to 3.8 %, and a minimum radiation field intensity of $U_{\mathrm{min}} = 10$.
We also adopt the Kroupa IMF which is corrected for unresolved binaries (cite: Kroupa2001; Kroupa2002), which was used to compute the integrated magnitudes.

fitting.value: Log-linear regression between L_Halpha,corr and nu L_nu,21um; Pareto-lognormal PDF fit to luminosity distributions with bootstrap resampling for slope uncertainties

evidence.quote: We fit a linear relation in log space between the attenuation-corrected HST H$\alpha$ luminosity and the F2100W luminosity

The uncertainties in the slope ($\beta$) were estimated for each galaxy using bootstrap by resampling the luminosity, and the standard deviation of the slopes derived from the Pareto–lognormal fits was reported as the error in $\beta$.

validation.value: Validated stellar color cuts against SAGE-LMC spectroscopically classified stars and cross-matched exposed clusters with MUSE nebular catalog

evidence.quote: We further compare the colors of our sources to SAGE-LMC sources in Figure [18](#fig:class_figure), finding good agreement for RSGs and O-AGBs using the color criteria F200W$-$F360M $< -0.3$ and F200W$-$F770W $< -1.8$ (see black solid lines in Figure [18](#fig:class_figure)).

By cross-matching our exposed sources with the “nebular” catalog from (cite: neb_catalog) using a maximum separation of 1$''$ (comparable to the typical MUSE PSF), we find that about 77% of the exposed clusters are associated with MUSE nebular regions across our sample of 19 galaxies.

used_for.value: JWST NIRCam and MIRI data reduction pipeline

evidence.quote: We use the data reduction pipeline `pjpipe`, described in (cite: Williams2024), which reduces $1/f$ noise in NIRCam, improves background flux consistency, and provides better calibration for both relative and absolute astrometry compared to MAST images

used_for.value: Convolving JWST and HST maps to match F1130W (0.36'') and F2100W (0.67'') resolutions

evidence.quote: For a 10 $\mu$m catalog, all maps are convolved to match the resolution of the F1130W filter (0.36$''$) using the `jwst_kernels` code.

used_for.value: Generating MUSE emission line maps and modeling stellar continuum

evidence.quote: For this work, we use emission line maps from (cite: phangs-muse), which were generated using the MUSE Data Analysis Pipeline (DAP).

used_for.value: Generating MIRI PSF masks for saturated galaxy centers and calculating PSF solid angles for photometry

evidence.quote: Hence we used STPSF (cite: Perrin) to generate a PSF matching the pixel scale of the MIRI images, positioned it at the center of the galaxy oriented to match the saturated sources, and subsequently applied a mask to the images.

After subtracting the median background, we convert the background-subtracted surface brightness to flux units ($\mu$Jy) by multiplying it by the solid angle subtended by the target PSF (see Table 4 of (cite: lee2023)), which was calculated using the STPSF package (cite: Perrin).

used_for.value: Dendrogram-based source identification in F1000W, F2100W, and F200W images

evidence.quote: We use the ASTRODENDRO package to identify and measure the structure of mid-infrared emission peaks.
For this analysis, we apply our `AstroDendo`-based source finder to F200W images, which have a FWHM of 0.067$''$  and considering a resolution element with 7 pixels, with a `minimum-beam=3`.

used_for.value: Generating simulated PSFs for artificial source tests

evidence.quote: First, using the PSF provided by the WEBBPSF package, we regridded the circularized PSF from 0.2$''$ to align with the MIRI pixel scale of 0.11$''$.

used_for.value: Modeling SEDs of dusty young stellar clusters

claims.hypothesis: The infrared-bright, optically faint (embedded) phase of young cluster evolution is short compared to the Halpha-bright (exposed) phase.
claims.experiment: Classify ISM-dominated compact sources in the 10 and 21 um catalogs into exposed and embedded clusters based on HST Halpha detection above completeness limits.
claims.result: Embedded (Halpha-faint) clusters account for <5% of the whole catalogs and only 5% (at 10 um) to 10% (at 21 um) of dusty ISM sources.
claims.finding: The infrared-bright, optically faint phase of cluster evolution is short compared to the Halpha-bright stage.

evidence.quote: We find that H$\alpha$-faint sources account for only 10% of dusty (likely young) clusters, implying that the infrared-bright, optically faint phase of cluster evolution is short compared to the H$\alpha$-bright stage.

If we restrict our analysis to ISM sources, 5% and 10% of them are identified as embedded clusters in the 10 $\mu$m and 21 $\mu$m catalogs, consistent with the findings for four galaxies in (cite: hassani23).

claims.hypothesis: The luminosity functions of 10 and 21 um compact ISM sources trace distinct structural scales of star formation and correlate with global galaxy star formation properties.
claims.experiment: Fit Pareto-lognormal probability density functions to the 10 and 21 um ISM source luminosity distributions across 19 galaxies and correlate slopes with Sigma_SFR.
claims.result: The median power-law slope is -1.73 +/- 0.10 at 21 um (correlating strongly with Sigma_SFR, rho = 0.86) and -2.02 +/- 0.03 at 10 um.
claims.finding: The 21 um luminosity function slope resembles GMC mass functions and HII region / UV star-forming complex luminosity functions and correlates with Sigma_SFR, whereas the steeper 10 um slope is closer to that of young stellar clusters.

evidence.quote: The luminosity functions of 10 and 21 $\mu$m sources follow power-law distributions, with the 21 $\mu$m slope ($-1.7 \pm 0.1$) similar to that of giant molecular cloud mass functions and ultraviolet bright star-forming complexes, while the 10 $\mu$m slope ($-2.0 \pm 0.1$) is closer to that of young stellar clusters.
We find that the 21 $\mu$m LF slopes correlate well with the star formation rate surface density ($\Sigma_\mathrm{SFR}$), with $\rho=0.86$ ($p < 10^{-5}$).

claims.hypothesis: Mid-infrared F2100W luminosity of young clusters correlates tightly with attenuation-corrected Halpha luminosity across galactic environments.
claims.experiment: Perform log-linear regression between attenuation-corrected HST Halpha luminosity and F2100W luminosity for 6,324 clusters across sub-galactic environments.
claims.result: Strong correlation (rho = 0.88 overall, scatter ~0.30 dex) with a sub-linear overall slope of 0.84 +/- 0.01 (ranging from 0.70 in bar ends to 0.91 in bars and disks) and a nearly constant median log ratio of 0.10 to 0.16.
claims.finding: Attenuation-corrected Halpha and 21 um luminosities follow a tight sub-linear relation over five orders of magnitude with minimal variation in the median ratio across galactic environments.

evidence.quote: Similar to (cite: hassani23), we find a strong correlation ($\rho > 0.8$) spanning five orders of magnitude between the H$\alpha$ attenuation-corrected luminosity and the F2100W luminosity.

The slope varies between 0.70 and 0.91 across different galactic environments: it is flatter in spiral arms and bar ends (which host more dusty, young clusters), steeper in the bars and disks, and intermediate in the central regions.

why_this_data.value: JWST NIRCam/MIRI provides the resolution and sensitivity needed to isolate compact mid-IR star-forming regions and dusty evolved stars in galaxies at 5-20 Mpc, complemented by PHANGS HST, MUSE, and ALMA CO(2-1) data.

evidence.quote: New observations with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) provide an opportunity to isolate and characterize high mass star-forming regions and bright, dusty stars in in more distant targets.

These observations and catalog are part of the Physics at High Angular Resolution in Nearby GalaxieS (PHANGS) survey, which also provides high resolution ancillary data of molecular gas from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (cite: Leroy2021)

why_this_method.value: Constrained Diffusion removes diffuse mid-IR background while preserving flux and non-negativity without wavelet artifacts, and ASTRODENDRO captures hierarchically nested and irregular mid-IR structures better than CLUMPFIND or SExtractor.

evidence.quote: In this study, we use Constrained Diffusion (cite: Li2022), a related approach that ensures the sum of all decomposed component fluxes matches the original input map and are non-negative.
Given the limitations of the source-finding algorithms discussed above, we adopt a dendrogram-based approach for source identification, following (cite: Williams) and (cite: hassani23).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Fourier filtering and wavelets for diffuse emission subtraction (rejected because they produce negative, non-physical artifacts in high-contrast areas)

evidence.quote: However, these methods can produce artifacts in decomposed maps, especially in areas with large contrasts in emission, resulting in negative, non-physical emission (cite: Coifman1995).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Convolving F2100W maps to 0.85'' resolution before CD filtering (rejected because it degrades physical resolution by 20 pc in the most distant targets)

evidence.quote: Despite this advantage, the convolution to 0.85$\ensuremath{''}$ introduces a 20 pc increase in physical resolution for the most distant targets. Given this limitation, we opted to use the filtered, native-resolution maps.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: CLUMPFIND, FELLWALKER, and SEXTRACTOR for source finding (rejected because CLUMPFIND blends diffuse emission and SEXTRACTOR struggles with irregular structures)

evidence.quote: In the case that medium consists of structured diffuse emission blended with compact sources, CLUMPFIND will often identify larger structures that reflect the diffuse emission rather than cleanly isolating the compact sources (cite: Williams).
Other algorithms, such as SEXTRACTOR (cite: Bertin), are better suited for identifying elliptical sources but struggle with irregular structures (cite: Williams).

limitations_admitted.value: Constrained Diffusion can fragment saturated sources and exacerbate diffraction spike artifacts in galaxy centers (requiring 18'' central masks in NGC 1365 and NGC 7496).

evidence.quote: However, one limitation is that saturated sources may be fragmented into several parts, where the wings and core of the PSF blend together, potentially confusing the source detection algorithm.

Additionally, this method can exacerbate diffraction spike artifacts in the central region of galaxies and result in numerous false detections, notably impacting two of our targets: NGC 1365 and NGC 7496.

limitations_admitted.value: Varying noise levels and distances (5-20 Mpc) across the 19 galaxies result in non-homogeneous sensitivity and luminosity detection thresholds, limiting RSG and O-AGB detection in more distant galaxies.

evidence.quote: We note that since the “step” values vary for each galaxy, the corresponding noise levels and detection limits also differ across our sample, resulting in a non-homogeneous sensitivity.

While many types of evolved stars are expected to be detectable in this nearby galaxy, we are unlikely to detect RSGs and O-rich AGBs in our more distant targets ($D\gtrsim 10~\mathrm{Mpc})$ (see Section [4.3.1](#sec:rsg-oagbs) for discussion).

limitations_admitted.value: PAH ionization and destruction processes are not included in the CIGALE cluster models, and the post-AGB phase is not included in the PARSEC models.

evidence.quote: PAH destruction processes are not included in our current modeling of young clusters.
We note that the post-AGB phase is not included in our `PARSEC` models, limiting our ability to estimate the properties of these stars.

limitations_admitted.value: CPNe and C-PAGB stars have overlapping infrared colors and cannot be distinguished with the current NIRCam and MIRI filter sets.

evidence.quote: Some bright C-PAGB sources can exhibit $r_7 > 1$, making it difficult to distinguish CPNs from C-PAGBs with the current NIRCam and MIRI filter sets.
Given these overlaps, we treat CPNe and C-PAGB candidates as a blended category.

limitations_admitted.value: MUSE spectral coverage and AO laser gaps limit optical spectroscopic confirmation of Wolf-Rayet Blue Bump and Red Bump features.

evidence.quote: While we do have optical spectroscopy of our targets from MUSE, our spectral coverage is not well suited for WR identification.

referee_caveats_inferred: Physical resolution varies by a factor of ~4 across the sample (5.2 to 19.6 Mpc), meaning 'compact' sources at ~20 Mpc (~60 pc) can blend multiple clusters and evolved stars that would be resolved in NGC 5068.

A few typos exist in the text and tables (e.g., Table 1 swaps the F1000W and F2100W column values for matched flux ranges, and a couple of LaTeX macros for source counts in Sections 4.3.2-4.3.5 failed to render in the text).
